terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. run.js starts the cupboard server, runs your functions against it and prints every request and answer.

tasks.title: Name the family of a status
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/statuses.js`, make `statusFamily(status)` take a status number and give back the name of its family as text: `'information'` for 100 to 199, `'success'` for 200 to 299, `'redirect'` for 300 to 399, `'client error'` for 400 to 499, `'server error'` for 500 to 599, and `'unknown'` for anything else.

Check calls `statusFamily` with statuses of its own, at the edges of the families and outside them.
nextSteps: Start with the numbers that are in no family at all.
Work out the family from the first digit of the status, as the lesson shows.
Give back the name with the exact words of the task.
Run `node run.js` and read the five Task 1 lines.
hints: The first digit of a status names its family. 100 to 599 are the statuses that have one.
`Math.floor(status / 100)` gives the first digit of a three digit number. You can compare it with `===`, or use it to pick from a list of the five names.
Return `'unknown'` when `status < 100 || status > 599`. Otherwise keep the names in a list, in order, and return the one at `Math.floor(status / 100) - 1`.

tasks.title: Read a show, or say why not
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make `showText(base, slug)` ask the server at `base` for the page `/shows/<slug>` and decide by the family of the answer's status:

- success: give back the text of the body
- client error: give back `null`, because the show is not there for this request
- server error: throw an `Error` whose message has the status number in it

Check starts a server of its own that answers with statuses from each family, and looks at the request its server received and at what `showText` gave back or threw.
nextSteps: Send the request and wait for the answer.
Work out the family of its status; your function from Task 1 can do that.
Give back the body, or `null`, or throw, as the task lists.
Run `node run.js`: one show is there, one is not, and the test card breaks the server.
hints: `fetch` does not fail on a 404 or a 500, so the decision is yours, made from `response.status`.
Read the body only in the success family. `throw new Error(message)` stops the function at once and hands the error to whoever called it.

After `const family = statusFamily(response.status)`, return the body when it is `'success'`, return `null` when it is `'client error'`, and when it is `'server error'`, `throw new Error(`The server answered ${response.status}`)`.

tasks.title: Ask again when the server is in trouble
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make `fetchWithRetry(address, tries)` ask for the page at `address`. While the answer is in the server error family, it asks again, sending at most `tries` requests in all. An answer from any other family is final at once. It gives back `{ status, body }` of the last answer it got.

Check starts a server of its own that answers 500s, 502s and 503s before it recovers, or never recovers, or answers 404, and counts the requests its server received.
nextSteps: Send the first request and keep the answer in a `let`.
Write a loop that asks again while the answer is a server error.
Count the requests, and stop the loop when the count reaches `tries`.
Return the status and the body of the last answer, then run `node run.js`.
hints: A loop that asks again needs two reasons to stop: an answer that is not a server error, and running out of tries.
A `while` loop with both conditions joined by `&&` stops as soon as either one is false. Count the requests in a variable that starts at 1 after the first one.
`while (statusFamily(response.status) === 'server error' && sent < tries) { response = await fetch(address); sent += 1 }`, then return `{ status: response.status, body: await response.text() }`.
